newsitem.title: UK: Wilde the new Oscar winner in Britain.
newsitem.headline: Wilde the new Oscar winner in Britain.

text.p: Flamboyant Irish playwright Oscar Wilde, who died penniless and in disgrace for his homosexuality, is being feted on both stage and screen in Britain.
For the tragic life of the Victorian genius who fell so dramatically from grace has given two of Britain's most famous gay actors the chance to pay homage to their hero.

Simon Callow has opened to rave reviews in London's theatreland with his one-man show "The Importance of Being Oscar" while Stephen Fry is filming a biography of the caustic playwright famed for his witticisms.
The Wilde renaissance would have delighted the foppish writer who once complained: "There is only one thing worse than being talked about and that is not being talked about."
The Dubliner shocked Victorian society over his affair with the Marquis of Queensberry's son, Lord Alfred Douglas. Wilde was sentenced to two years in jail for gross indecency.
The author of such comic classics as "The Importance of Being Earnest" and "Lady Windermere's Fan" died a broken man in 1900 at the age of 46.
Callow, famed for his role as the homosexual lover in the hit film "Four Weddings and a Funeral", has always idolised Wilde.
"This was the man I wanted to be, generous, eloquent, intellectually brilliant, provocative, fun and of course gay -- though I kept rather quiet about that bit. This was, after all, 1963," he said.
As a student in Belfast, Callow even wrote a play about Wilde and "I sat around talking in what I imagined was a Wildean fashion, epigrams tumbling out of my mouth."
Fry, himself notorious for abandoning the play "Cell Mates" in the middle of a London run when he vanished and had a nervous breakdown, is equally wild about Oscar.

The heavily-built comedian said: "I've been researching Wilde all my life. I've been passionate about him since I was 11. He teaches me to take the serious things in life trivially and the trivial things seriously."
"He stands for all people who refused to freeze themselves into a moral code," he said.
The film, unlike two earlier "biopics" starring Robert Morley and Peter Finch, is much more explicit in its homosexual scenes.
But the film, based on Richard Ellmann's acclaimed biography, seeks to balance the picture by stressing Wilde's love for his wife Constance and their two sons who fled abroad under assumed names.
Wilde's grandson, Merlin Holland, thoroughly approves and offers one of the playwright's letters to a London court as the most fitting epitaph:
"I do hope the court will see in me something more than a man with a tragic vice in his life. There is so much more in me and I was always a good father to both my children.
"I loved them dearly and was loved by them. It would be better for them to be forced to think of me not as an outcast but to know me as a man who has suffered."
